3. Bayesian calibrations and reconstructions

Source: vignettes/bayesian.Rmd
bayesian.Rmd

This vignette covers Bayesian calibrations in bayclumpr. We fit the models, choose priors, check convergence, compare models, and reconstruct temperatures. If you’re new to the package, start with vignette("bayclumpr", package = "bayclumpr").

library(bayclumpr)

The four models

cal.bayesian() fits up to four models. They cover every combination of two choices: whether measurement errors are used, and whether intercepts and slopes vary by Material. We choose them with the models argument.

models Name in the result Measurement errors Varies by Material
"errors" BLM1_fit Yes No
"noerrors" BLM1_fit_NoErrors No No
"mixed_errors" BLM3_fit_Errors Yes Yes
"mixed_noerrors" BLM3_fit No Yes

Models with measurement errors use TempError and D47error for each observation. All models estimate sigma, the scatter around the calibration line. With measurement errors, sigma is the scatter left after removing the measurement error in D47. Without them, it includes the measurement error.

Mixed models let intercepts and slopes vary by Material around shared means. They need at least two materials and are skipped otherwise.

The models run in Stan. If they weren’t compiled when bayclumpr was installed, the first fit of each model in a session compiles it. This can take a minute or more. Later fits in the same session start right away.

Fitting a model

We simulate 50 observations under the intermediate error scenario. The true values are alpha = 0.268 and beta = 0.0369.

set.seed(3)
ds <- cal.dataset(error = "S2", nobs = 50)

We start with the errors model:

fit <- cal.bayesian(calibrationData = ds, models = "errors")
#> Compiling the Stan model errors. This happens once per session and can take a minute or two.
fit
#> Bayesian clumped isotope calibration
#> Priors: alpha ~ N(0.231, 0.065), beta ~ N(0.039, 0.004)
#> 
#> BLM1_fit
#>  parameter estimate       SE  median   lower   upper  ESS   Rhat
#>      alpha  0.25881 0.020695 0.25869 0.21710 0.29843 4058 0.9997
#>       beta  0.03750 0.001717 0.03749 0.03419 0.04095 3997 0.9995
#>      sigma  0.02463 0.002906 0.02439 0.01948 0.03066 4750 0.9991
#> 
#> Convergence
#>     model max_Rhat min_ESS divergences
#>  BLM1_fit   0.9997    3997           0

The first table is the same summary given by cal.summary(). estimate is the posterior mean of each parameter and SE is its standard error, which is the SD of the posterior draws. sigma is itself an SD: the scatter of individual samples around the calibration line. ESS and Rhat show how well each parameter was sampled. The second table checks convergence for each model as a whole. We look for max_Rhat at or below 1.01, min_ESS of at least 100 per chain, and no divergences. cal.bayesian() gives a warning when a model fails any of these checks. When that happens, try a larger numSavedSteps and check the data for outliers or wrong units.

Choosing priors

The priors argument sets the priors on alpha and beta. There are three presets:

priors alpha beta
"Informative" Normal(0.231, 0.065) Normal(0.039, 0.004)
"Weak" Normal(0.231, 1) Normal(0.039, 1)
"Flat" Flat Flat

The informative values are the ones used in earlier versions of this package. Calibrations differ among reference frames and acid corrections, so check that these values suit your data. You can also set your own priors as a list with the mean and SD of each normal prior:

myPriors <- list(alpha = c(0.25, 0.05), beta = c(0.038, 0.003))

cal.prior() draws from a set of priors. This shows the range of slopes that a prior allows before seeing the data:

quantile(cal.prior("Informative", n = 10000)$beta, c(0.025, 0.975))
#>       2.5%      97.5% 
#> 0.03105497 0.04668649
quantile(cal.prior(myPriors, n = 10000)$beta, c(0.025, 0.975))
#>       2.5%      97.5% 
#> 0.03203628 0.04367196

Let’s fit the same model under weak priors and compare the slopes:

fitWeak <- cal.bayesian(calibrationData = ds, models = "errors", priors = "Weak")

rbind(
  Informative = quantile(cal.draws(fit)$beta, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  Weak = quantile(cal.draws(fitWeak)$beta, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
)
#>                   2.5%        50%      97.5%
#> Informative 0.03419203 0.03748993 0.04094567
#> Weak        0.03260000 0.03677161 0.04075844

Comparing models

We can fit several models at once and compare them with cal.compare(). It uses approximate leave-one-out cross-validation.

fits <- cal.bayesian(calibrationData = ds, models = c("errors", "noerrors"))
#> Compiling the Stan model noerrors. This happens once per session and can take a minute or two.
cal.compare(fits)
#>              model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff diag_elpd
#>  BLM1_fit_NoErrors       0.0     0.0      NA                    
#>           BLM1_fit      -0.1     0.1    0.89   N < 100
#> 
#> Diagnostic flags present.
#> See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
#> or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.

The best model is in the first row. When elpd_diff is small relative to se_diff, the data don’t clearly favor one model.

Mixed models

To show the mixed models, we simulate a second material with D47 values that are 0.02 higher:

ds1 <- cal.dataset(error = "S2", nobs = 50)
ds2 <- cal.dataset(error = "S2", nobs = 50)
ds2$D47 <- ds2$D47 + 0.02
ds2$Material <- 2
dsMixed <- rbind(ds1, ds2)

fitMixed <- cal.bayesian(calibrationData = dsMixed, models = c("mixed_errors", "mixed_noerrors"))
#> Compiling the Stan model mixed_errors. This happens once per session and can take a minute or two.
#> Warning: There were 24 divergent transitions after warmup. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup
#> to find out why this is a problem and how to eliminate them.
#> Warning: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
#> Compiling the Stan model mixed_noerrors. This happens once per session and can take a minute or two.
#> Warning: There were 23 divergent transitions after warmup. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup
#> to find out why this is a problem and how to eliminate them.
#> Warning: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
#> Warning: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bulk-ess
#> Warning: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#tail-ess
#> Warning in .finish_fit(fits, prior, chains): Check convergence for: BLM3_fit_Errors,
#> BLM3_fit. Print the result for details.
fitMixed
#> Bayesian clumped isotope calibration
#> Priors: alpha ~ N(0.231, 0.065), beta ~ N(0.039, 0.004)
#> 
#> BLM3_fit_Errors
#>  Material parameter estimate       SE  median   lower   upper  ESS   Rhat
#>         1     alpha  0.26988 0.016214 0.26962 0.23926 0.30229 2692 1.0018
#>         1      beta  0.03747 0.001399 0.03748 0.03463 0.04016 2708 1.0017
#>         1     sigma  0.02435 0.001956 0.02421 0.02084 0.02837 3976 1.0006
#>         2     alpha  0.26863 0.021463 0.26867 0.22481 0.31017 2938 0.9994
#>         2      beta  0.03833 0.001765 0.03833 0.03483 0.04192 2946 0.9994
#>         2     sigma  0.02435 0.001956 0.02421 0.02084 0.02837 3976 1.0006
#> 
#> BLM3_fit
#>  Material parameter estimate       SE  median   lower   upper  ESS   Rhat
#>         1     alpha  0.27035 0.016371 0.26990 0.23813 0.30256 2891 0.9995
#>         1      beta  0.03744 0.001407 0.03745 0.03462 0.04016 2947 0.9997
#>         1     sigma  0.02570 0.001887 0.02558 0.02224 0.02966 1739 1.0034
#>         2     alpha  0.26913 0.021344 0.26930 0.22539 0.31011 2812 0.9992
#>         2      beta  0.03828 0.001749 0.03827 0.03488 0.04184 2897 0.9993
#>         2     sigma  0.02570 0.001887 0.02558 0.02224 0.02966 1739 1.0034
#> 
#> Convergence
#>            model max_Rhat min_ESS divergences
#>  BLM3_fit_Errors    1.002    2692          24
#>         BLM3_fit    1.003    1739          23

The intercepts and slopes of the two materials are pulled toward shared means (partial pooling). The SDs among materials have half-normal priors with scales of 0.1 for the intercept at the mean calibration temperature and 0.01 for the slope. With fewer than five materials, these SDs mostly reflect their priors.

Reconstructing temperatures

cal.draws() returns the posterior draws of a model as a table. It has the same columns as the frequentist tables in vignette("frequentist", package = "bayclumpr").

draws <- cal.draws(fit)
head(draws)
#>       alpha       beta      sigma
#> 1 0.2913857 0.03403879 0.02635096
#> 2 0.2286358 0.03961537 0.02440160
#> 3 0.2765121 0.03592458 0.02101763
#> 4 0.2381617 0.03879429 0.02470852
#> 5 0.2492998 0.03765331 0.01982520
#> 6 0.2539153 0.03745754 0.02471296

We create a reconstruction dataset and pass it to rec.bayesian() with the draws:

recData <- data.frame(
  Sample = paste("Sample", 1:6),
  D47 = rep(c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8), 2),
  D47error = rep(c(0.005, 0.02), each = 3),
  N = 3
)

rec.bayesian(calModel = draws, recData = recData)
#>     Sample D47 D47error  meanTemp        SD        SE     median      lower     upper
#> 1 Sample 1 0.6    0.005 59.169525 13.492686 12.919351  58.141071  36.176558 86.901763
#> 2 Sample 2 0.7    0.005 18.679092  8.878960  8.507950  18.238345   2.936739 36.380216
#> 3 Sample 3 0.8    0.005 -9.781490  6.594663  6.322624  -9.933485 -21.692635  3.210007
#> 4 Sample 4 0.6    0.020 59.489531 21.596755 16.403661  58.415102  30.709281 95.152623
#> 5 Sample 5 0.7    0.020 18.852540 14.311770 10.866998  18.135342  -0.351929 42.237888
#> 6 Sample 6 0.8    0.020 -9.734762 10.696587  7.841322 -10.021680 -24.568806  5.917603

meanTemp is the posterior mean temperature in °C. SE is the standard error of the temperature, based on D47error, the standard error of the mean D47. SD is the uncertainty of the temperature of a single replicate, based on D47error × sqrt(N). SD is NA when the dataset has neither N nor D47sd. median, lower, and upper describe the 95% posterior interval, based on SE. Both SD and SE include the calibration, the scatter around the calibration line (sigma), and the error in D47. rec.clumped() gives the same kind of uncertainty with prediction = TRUE.

rec.bayesian() doesn’t run another MCMC. For each posterior draw, the temperature has a known distribution, so it’s sampled directly. This takes less than a second.

We can also pass the result of cal.bayesian() and name the model:

rec.bayesian(calModel = fits, recData = recData, model = "noerrors")
#>     Sample D47 D47error  meanTemp        SD        SE     median       lower     upper
#> 1 Sample 1 0.6    0.005 59.582528 13.850920 13.356362  58.760144  35.6641789 87.739793
#> 2 Sample 2 0.7    0.005 18.738866  9.209379  8.807402  18.453100   2.3154928 36.871627
#> 3 Sample 3 0.8    0.005 -9.680912  6.965055  6.621272  -9.908738 -22.0689063  3.782275
#> 4 Sample 4 0.6    0.020 59.743116 22.361167 16.759462  58.531780  30.6149554 95.806125
#> 5 Sample 5 0.7    0.020 19.093028 14.569364 10.940762  18.535532  -0.3365017 42.545939
#> 6 Sample 6 0.8    0.020 -9.661798 10.738637  8.158392 -10.011537 -24.7372205  6.941973

Reconstructions with mixed models

For mixed models, the reconstruction dataset needs a Material column with the same labels used in the calibration:

recMixed <- data.frame(
  Sample = c("Sample 1", "Sample 2"),
  D47 = c(0.62, 0.62),
  D47error = 0.01,
  Material = c(1, 2)
)

rec.bayesian(calModel = fitMixed, recData = recMixed, model = "mixed_errors")
#>     Sample  D47 D47error meanTemp SD       SE   median    lower    upper
#> 1 Sample 1 0.62     0.01 54.89756 NA 12.72386 54.08777 32.33342 82.54673
#> 2 Sample 2 0.62     0.01 58.08932 NA 13.09937 57.30202 34.82513 86.17134

Mixed models can also reconstruct temperatures for a material that is not in the calibration. With newMaterial = TRUE, the intercept and slope are drawn from the shared means and the spread among materials. The intervals are wider, since we don’t know where the new material falls among the others.

recNew <- data.frame(Sample = "Sample 3", D47 = 0.62, D47error = 0.01)
rec.bayesian(calModel = fitMixed, recData = recNew, model = "mixed_errors", newMaterial = TRUE)
#> Warning in .rec_exact(draws, recData, ndraws, level = level): 27 draws had 10^6/T^2 at or
#> below zero and were removed.
#>     Sample  D47 D47error meanTemp SD       SE   median    lower    upper
#> 1 Sample 3 0.62     0.01 60.44808 NA 62.03957 54.12968 9.942506 136.8542

Tips for faster fits

  • Fit only the models you need with the models argument.
  • Run chains in parallel with cores, for example cores = 4.
  • Use fewer draws while you explore, for example numSavedSteps = 1000, and more for final results.
